chunks: Where data and program live. The question: Where can data and program be stored in memory?
A program and its data are both just patterns of bits, so they can sit in any memory in the system.
Memories differ in speed, size, and whether they keep their contents with the power off. The program is usually stored in memory that survives power loss.
Values that change while it runs live in fast memory that forgets.
Think of an office. The filing cabinet holds everything permanently, but digging through it is slow.
Your desk holds what you are working on, and it is cleared when you leave for the night. Your hands hold the one or two things you are using this second.
The cabinet is flash or disk, the desk is RAM (such as SRAM), and your hands are the CPU's registers.
The same flat address space routes to different physical blocks.
Flash (green) holds code, constants and the initial values of globals; SRAM (blue) holds everything that changes; peripheral registers (orange) look like memory but are hardware control points.
The curved arrow is the startup copy of . data .
Non-volatile: keeps its contents with the power off. Volatile memory forgets them. Flash: non-volatile memory that holds the program and constants.
It reads fast but is slow to rewrite. SRAM: fast, volatile memory for variables that change.
Register: a tiny storage slot inside the CPU that holds the value being worked on right now. Startup code: the first code to run after reset, which prepares memory.
A small chip has 64 KB of flash and 20 KB of SRAM. The program code is 38 KB, constants such as lookup tables are 6 KB, and the starting values of variables are 1 KB.
Flash holds 38 plus 6 plus 1 equals 45 KB. At power-up, the startup code copies those 1 KB of starting values into SRAM.
SRAM also holds 3 KB of variables that start at zero, so 4 KB in all.
That leaves 16 KB for the stack (scratch space for function calls) and the heap (memory a program asks for while running). That is the whole idea.
"Program and data are both just bits, so they can live in registers, caches, SRAM, DRAM, flash and disk. At rest the program sits in non-volatile memory like flash or an SSD.
When it runs, instructions and data are brought into RAM and then into caches and registers.
On a microcontroller, code and constants stay in flash, variables and the stack live in SRAM, and the startup code copies initialized globals from flash into RAM.
Von Neumann machines share one memory for both, Harvard machines keep them separate."
